documents: Ramp et al. 2022, Nonlin. Processes Geophys. 29, 279-299, published PDF
Publisher full text from XML with section and paragraph locators (jats_text)

entry.evidence: (1) how are NLIWs transformed as they shoal over a gentle slope between 388 and 266 m over the continental slope?

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text, PDF for figures)

steps.action: The study starts from the discovery of large undersea sand dunes on the slope, reported in earlier work co-authored by Reeder and Yang, and mapped further by MBES surveys.
steps.quote: The present study was motivated by the discovery of large ( h > 15 m, λ order 350 m) undersea sand dunes

steps.action: The authors pose questions on how NLIWs transform as they shoal over the gentle dune-field slope and which mechanisms are responsible.
steps.quote: (1) how are NLIWs transformed as they shoal over a gentle slope between 388 and 266 m over the continental slope?

steps.action: They design and deploy four closely spaced moorings across the slope, with T/S sampled every 60 s, 15-30 m vertical spacing and ADCPs, at rates chosen to avoid aliasing.
steps.quote: An array of four oceanographic moorings were deployed across the continental slope

steps.action: An MBES survey characterizes the dune field and the sharp change in bottom slope (1:35 versus 1:160) that frames the comparison with theory.
steps.quote: the most important fact about the bottom is the sharp, clear change of bottom slope across the dotted white line (Fig. 2)

steps.action: With no remote observations, barotropic tidal forcing in the Luzon Strait is taken from the TPXO7.0 global tidal model, previously validated against observations.
steps.quote: barotropic tidal forcing in the Luzon Strait as obtained from the TPXO7.0 global tidal model

steps.action: All NLIW arrivals over the 18-day live record are identified from the 20 °C isotherm displacement at RPO and labelled as a/b (A/B) waves.
steps.quote: A total of 21 NLIWs with amplitude greater than 20 m were observed, 13 a waves and 8 b waves.

steps.action: Wave amplitudes, lagged by 48.5 h, are compared with the TPXO fortnightly tidal envelope: they track spring-neap forcing, the major beats, and the ebb tide for a waves.
steps.quote: First, the NLIW amplitudes at RPO track the fortnightly tidal amplitudes in the Luzon Strait.

steps.action: The apparent alignment of b waves with the major flood tide is rejected as coincidence, using unshown directional histograms that point to a separate, closer northern source.
steps.quote: the b waves were sometimes aligned well with the major flood tide preceding each a wave, but we now believe this to be coincidence

steps.action: The 2-6 June sequence across all four moorings establishes local b-wave formation by steepening and breaking of the internal-tide front between YPO1 and RPO.
steps.quote: This example thus demonstrates a local b-wave formation process via steepening of the leading edge of the tidal front.

steps.action: Amplitudes across the four moorings (Fig. 8) show smaller waves gaining amplitude upslope and waves larger than about 50 m losing it.
steps.quote: All waves larger than about 50 m offshore (13–18 June) lost amplitude as they shoaled, most clearly between CPO and RPO

steps.action: The amplitude pattern is compared with numerical results of Lamb and Warn-Varnas (2015) and with EKdV theory, and found consistent.
steps.quote: This result is consistent with the numerical results of Lamb and Warn-Varnas (2015)

steps.action: Waves B9, A9 and A9' and their packet structure are checked against independent MODIS ocean-colour imagery taken as A9 reached YPO2.
steps.quote: Waves B9, A9, and A9' can be clearly seen in the satellite ocean color imagery (Fig. 9).

steps.action: Velocity and temperature sections across the array contrast a weakly forced (3-4 June) and a strongly forced (16-17 June) case: packet growth, nodal depth, and b waves at the leading edge of the tide.
steps.quote: Two examples of velocity and temperature across the slope are shown to illustrate the difference between weakly and strongly forced waves.

steps.action: From laboratory and numerical studies, four rival transformation pathways are stated for the shoaling waves.
steps.quote: The possibilities include adiabatic shoaling, dispersion, breaking, and conversion to waves of elevation.

steps.action: Conversion to elevation waves is excluded because the KdV critical point lies well inshore of the array.
steps.quote: The latter may be easily ruled out for this study

steps.action: The breaking criterion (Eq. 1) is evaluated with the observed thermocline depth (23 °C isotherm), giving required amplitudes of 112 m at CPO and 84 m at RPO.
steps.quote: Substituting these values in Eq. (1) shows that a wave amplitude of 112 m would be required at CPO for wave breaking to occur.

steps.action: Observed amplitudes are compared with the breaking thresholds; all fall below them, so breaking is not expected.
steps.quote: all the observed wave amplitudes were lower than the above criteria, and no wave breaking events are expected in this array.

steps.action: Detailed structure at RPO is examined for a typical a wave (A3, symmetric, u < c) and for the largest wave (A9, back-side steepening and a subsurface velocity maximum near c).
steps.quote: The largest wave observed was wave A9 on 17 June. This wave showed several characteristics of breaking or near-breaking waves (Fig. 13).

steps.action: The subsurface velocity maximum is attributed partly to opposing cyclone-forced currents and a storm-deepened mixed layer that limits breaking, which protects the no-breaking reading.
steps.quote: It is worth noting that the subsurface velocity maximum in the wave may be caused by phenomena other than wave breaking.

steps.action: The observed trailing-wave and mode-2 pattern is compared with Lamb (2002) model runs that include a surface mixed layer, and found closely similar.
steps.quote: the scenario described above in the “Results” section rather closely resembles the model results of Lamb (2002) when a surface mixed layer was added

steps.action: The authors conclude that the packets formed upslope were made by dispersion, not breaking.
steps.quote: from YPO2 to RPO were formed by dispersion rather than wave breaking.

steps.action: Rotation as a local packet-forming mechanism is excluded from timescales (2 h versus a 32 h inertial period); undular bores were not observed.
steps.quote: [...] locally unimportant, given that the packets formed in just 2 h, while the local inertial period was 32 h.

steps.action: The local b-wave mechanism is refined: the waves form all at once by collision of the westward internal tide with the off-slope eastward tide.
steps.quote: The waves were formed all at once by the collision and breaking of the westward internal tide with the off-slope-propagating eastward tide.

steps.action: Theoretical expectations for energy partition are taken from the literature: KE/PE about 1.3 for solitary waves, and PE flux exceeding KE flux under shoaling.
steps.quote: For shoaling NLIW however, the flux of PE theoretically exceeds the flux of KE, which causes the PE to exceed the KE in shallower water

steps.action: Two ways of estimating density at the temperature-only moorings are benchmarked against observed salinity at RPO and CPO; ADCP gaps are filled by normal-mode fits, with the mode number chosen for stability.
steps.quote: The APE computed using the mean T / S curve was found to agree much better with the observations

steps.action: HKE, APE and the full nonlinear energy flux (pressure work plus advection terms) are computed from the moored data for each wave and mooring.
steps.quote: all three terms of the flux equation were computed.

steps.action: The energy partition across the slope is compared with theory: the incident HKE/APE ratio is 1.7 (above 1.3), with a shift to APE > HKE between CPO and RPO and total energy lost for the larger waves.
steps.quote: there was a dramatic change when the APE increased and the HKE sharply decreased

steps.action: The flux terms are decomposed (pressure work 43-57%), and the KE flux drop and slight PE flux rise from CPO to RPO are quantified.
steps.quote: From CPO to RPO, the kinetic energy flux dropped by 50 % (blue line to green line), while the potential energy flux went up slightly

steps.action: The amplitude-dependent transformation and energy results are kept as roughly agreeing with theory and simulations.
steps.quote: These results are in rough agreement with recent theory and numerical simulations of shoaling waves.

tree.answer: Shoaling NLIWs transform over a gentle, rough dune-field slope
Yes, by moored temperature, salinity and ADCP velocity
Describe the transformation and identify its mechanisms
Adiabatic shoaling, dispersion, breaking, conversion to elevation (and rotation)
Breaking amplitude thresholds (112 m, 84 m), u versus c, energy partition shift
Conditions found: natural wave arrivals over an 18-day record

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats: 21 waves over a spring-neap cycle at four moorings
Limited: density method benchmark and satellite cross-check; no formal sensitivity on the claims
Dispersion, not breaking, forms the packets; small waves shoal adiabatically

end.claim: Waves smaller than about 50 m and 100 MJ m-1 shoaled adiabatically, while larger waves formed packets by dispersion rather than breaking, with KE flux falling and PE flux rising slightly upslope.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing observed amplitudes and orbital velocities with the breaking criteria evaluated at CPO and RPO is what rules out breaking and leaves dispersion as the packet-forming mechanism.

gates.evidence: The moorings were placed to observe NLIWs shoaling over the dune field (§2 ¶1); no stated hypothesis directed the acquisition. The no-breaking claim faced a criterion it could have failed (§4.1 ¶2), but the largest wave A9 nearly met it and was explained by cyclone effects (§4.1 ¶5). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Korteweg-de Vries and extended KdV theory for solitary waves
Exact solutions of the fully nonlinear equations giving the KE/PE ratio of 1.3 (Turkington et al. 1991)

novelty_claims.quote: [...] different mechanism than that described for shoaling ISWs in the literature.
New information gleaned includes the packet formation process, further insights on the difference between a waves and b waves
but they did not make the connection to b-wave formation

limits: The review statement names an editor and two referees, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims sit at different statuses: the amplitude threshold (about 50 m, 100 MJ m-1) separating adiabatic from dispersive shoaling is a regularity_in_range over one 18-day record. Local b-wave formation by tidal-front convergence is a best_explanation from a few events. The energy and flux partitions are estimates given without uncertainties (estimate_with_resolution in form only). The directional histograms used to exclude the flood-tide alignment of b waves are not shown. The upper 20 m was unsampled, and CPO velocity gaps were filled by a three-mode fit. The origin of the double A waves is left unresolved. Composition is coded trace_series by best fit: conditions were found, not set, and the claim is the best among stated rivals. However, the observations are live repeated events rather than past traces, so natures_repetition is a near alternative (coder's inference). The 48.5 h lag adjustment is given no justification. Dissipation over the dunes is deferred to Helfrich et al. (2022, in review).

disagreements.target: Duda et al. (2004), ASIAEX bore-like features
disagreements.support: Moorings across the slope show the steepened tidal front breaking into b-wave packets, a connection the earlier study did not make.
disagreements.quote: was noted in the ASIAEX data (Duda et al., 2004), but they did not make the connection to b-wave formation

disagreements.target: Literature mechanisms for packet formation in shoaling ISWs
disagreements.support: b waves absent at YPO2 form packets by RPO through collision of westward and off-slope eastward internal tides.
disagreements.quote: [...] different mechanism than that described for shoaling ISWs in the literature.

disagreements.target: Theoretical KE/PE ratio of 1.3 (Turkington et al., 1991; Lamb and Nguyen, 2009)
disagreements.support: The observed incident HKE/APE averages 1.7 at YPO2, which is read as highly nonlinear waves.
disagreements.quote: This ratio is even larger than the theoretical expectation of 1.3

disagreements.target: Breaking at the 300 m isobath farther southwest (Chang et al., 2021b)
disagreements.support: Breaking criteria are not met at the dune site because amplitudes are smaller near the crests' northern extremity.
disagreements.quote: This situation contrasts with a similar depth range farther southwest, where larger waves were already actively breaking at the 300 m isobath

alternatives_considered.chosen: Mean T/S curves (pre- and post-storm) to infer salinity at YPO1 and YPO2
alternatives_considered.reason: APE from T/S curves agreed much better with observed-salinity density at RPO and CPO

alternatives_considered.chosen: Three normal modes for filling ADCP gaps
Full nonlinear flux including HKE and APE advection (Eq. 7)
alternatives_considered.reason: Not obvious that the linear approximation is valid for strongly nonlinear shoaling waves

alternatives_considered.chosen: Lag of 48.5 h from the Luzon Strait
alternatives_considered.alternatives: 50.3 h propagation time from a full year's data (Ramp et al., 2010)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Separate northern generation site for b waves
alternatives_considered.alternatives: b-wave generation aligned with the major flood tide
alternatives_considered.reason: Directional histograms show a waves about 24° more northward than b waves

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Wave breaking; rotation (trailing undular bores); conversion to elevation waves
alternatives_considered.reason: Amplitudes below the breaking criteria; packets form in 2 h versus a 32 h inertial period; critical point lies inshore
